newsitem.title: GERMANY: Search for EMU cash will lift German privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Search for EMU cash will lift German privatisation.

text.p: The hunt for cash to help Germany meet European monetary union targets will help boost Germany's privatisation programme and analysts said on Monday that markets are ready to snap up what Bonn puts up for sale.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel is gearing up to sell the family silver to help the country meet the Maastricht criteria on government debt and budget deficits to take part in European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
"The German government needs to sell things and they are prepared to do it. said Robert Willis, German analyst at Schroder Securities in London.
"Privatisation as a philosophy already has a German flavour with the privatisation of (formerly Communist state-owned assets in) East Germany," he added.
Britain and the U.S. are usually perceived as the world leaders in privatisation, with Germany again trailing the Anglo-Saxon business world when it comes to privatisation.

But this is image is not entirely fair on Germany, which oversaw one of the most comprehensive privatisation programmes ever when it effectively privatised the former East Germany following reunification in 1990.
The German government has a treasure trove of goodies to sell, including state banking interests, electricity providers and thousands of miles of autobahn (motorway).

A report in Monday's Handelsblatt newspaper said Waigel was looking to privatise the state's real estate holdings by selling them off to a private company, possibly to one of Germany's giant diversified utilities.
Earlier this year, Bonn sold the state property company Deutschbau to the property wing of diversified utility Veba AG for over two billion marks.
Central to the current programme of cutting debt and deficits is the sale of further chunks of the telecoms group Deutsche Telekom and airline Lufthansa AG.

There is speculation about when Bonn will sell the next tranche of Telekom, following the successful sale of the first 20-million-mark chunk in November last year, while it said that it plans to sell off the remainder of Lufthansa in the autumn.

However, a massive sell-off of state assets will not be a panacea for Germany's fiscal ills and will not help it meet the criterion in the Maastricht treaty which requires the ratio of government deficit to GDP to be less than 60 percent.
"One thing agreed on by everybody is that privatisation receipts will not help the deficit situation, but it will help relieve the debt situation," said one London-based analyst.
Earlier fears that the sale of a further massive chunk of Deutsche Telekom could flood the market with shares in the group seem overdone, analysts said.

The sell-off of France Telecom has been put on hold while the new left-wing government considers whether or not it wants to sell a stake in the company or whether it will keep the group as a state-owned asset.
This means many investors who had planned to invest in France Telecom are again looking at Deutsche Telekom.

It is likely the government will "park" the share packet with an government agency like the east German development agency KfW, which will not be allowed sell shares on the open market for a limited amount of time.
The agency in turn would receive the shares at a lower price and would probably be guaranteed a dividend payout.
"If Telekom stock is not put directly onto the market, then it won't put pressure on the share price," said Willis.

"A lot of news has already been digested and investors are taking a sober view on Telekom. If it is parked with an interim agency on condition that it won't be sold on the open market for a number of years, that could help the stock," said Willis.
This would allow investors to free up existing stock on the market, safe in the knowledge that more is on its way upon a certain date.
The health of the equity market means that the liquidity to absorb a series of privatisations is probably there.
As one analyst said: "The flow of funds into the German equity market is definitely healthy at the moment and is likely to stay that way.
